title: Time Zone Converter: Convert Times Worldwide
description: Convert a time between time zones with the Time Zone Converter — daylight saving handled, city to city, date line aware. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 9:00 a.m. in New York is 2:00 p.m. in London and 7:30 p.m. in Mumbai — the half-hour that reminds everyone India never does anything by halves.
quick_answer: The Time Zone Converter converts a time and date between zones — New York to London, Chicago to Berlin — applying each zone's real rules, including daylight saving. Enter the time and both zones and read the converted time, day shift included.

Departure in one zone, arrival in another, both printed in local time — the converter is how you learn you land 'before you left' (you did not; the date line did it).
Kickoffs, product drops and streams publish in one zone and are watched in fifty — convert the announcement once, correctly.
London to Sydney swings between 9 and 11 hours across the year — the converter absorbs the two hemispheres' opposite daylight-saving seasons.
9:00 New York (EST, winter) = 14:00 London = 15:00 Berlin = 19:30 Mumbai = 01:00 next day in Sydney (AEDT). One meeting, four dates' worth of arithmetic, one conversion.
For about three weeks each spring, the US has sprung forward but Europe has not: New York–London shrinks to 4 hours. Converters using fixed offsets get these weeks wrong; rule-based ones do not.

faq: What happens in the weeks when only one side has changed its clocks?

The gap between the zones temporarily grows or shrinks by an hour (New York–London is 4 hours, not 5, for about three weeks each spring). The converter applies each zone's rules for the exact date, so those weeks come out right.
Can I convert a whole schedule of times at once?

One time per conversion here — step through the schedule, or convert the anchor time and shift the rest by the same difference (valid until a clock-change date intervenes, which the single conversions reveal).
Does it need my location to work?
No — you name both zones explicitly, so the conversion is identical anywhere. Your location only matters if you ask for 'my time' as one of the zones.
Enough hours east or west crosses midnight — Sydney is routinely 'tomorrow' from the US. The converter shows the resulting date explicitly.
Handled — India (+5:30), Iran (+3:30) and Newfoundland (−3:30) among them; Nepal's +5:45 quarter-hour too.
What is UTC in all this?
The reference meridian time all offsets hang from — the World Time Zone Map shows the whole pattern at a glance.
No daylight saving there (nor in most of the tropics) — the rules know it even when visitors forget.
